A.explanation: Part of the $0.4L$ compression recovered and part remained permanent, so elastic and plastic deformation were both present at $0.6L$.

B.explanation: Elastic deformation alone would allow full recovery from $0.6L$ back to $L$, but the cylinder only recovered to $0.8L$.

C.explanation: Plastic deformation alone would give no recovery, but the length increased from $0.6L$ to $0.8L$ when forces were removed.

D.explanation: The change in length from $L$ to $0.6L$ and the partial recovery show deformation did occur.

hints: Compare the three lengths in the diagram: $L$ before loading, $0.6L$ under load, and $0.8L$ after unloading.
Any increase in length from $0.6L$ to $0.8L$ after the forces are removed must be recovered elastic deformation.
Any failure to return from $0.8L$ all the way to the original $L$ must be permanent plastic deformation.
walkthrough: Note the useful data: original length $L$, length under compressive force $0.6L$, length after force removed $0.8L$.
Recall the rule: elastic deformation is recovered on unloading, while plastic deformation remains as a permanent change.
Find the recovered part: $0.8L - 0.6L = 0.2L$ of extension occurred after unloading, so $0.2L$ of the compression at $0.6L$ was elastic.
Find the permanent part: $L - 0.8L = 0.2L$ of compression never recovered, so $0.2L$ of the compression at $0.6L$ was plastic.
Since the total compression at $0.6L$ was $L - 0.6L = 0.4L$, it consisted of $0.2L$ recoverable plus $0.2L$ permanent deformation.
Therefore the deformation at $0.6L$ was partly elastic and partly plastic. This is option A
